subChunks.title: From Senior Engineer to Lead: Multiplying Impact
subChunks.hookHtml: The most disorienting transition in a software career is from Senior Engineer to Lead. Your value no longer comes from the code you write — it comes from the outcomes your team achieves. Most engineers are never explicitly taught how to make this shift. This lesson is that teaching.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What Changes at Lead Level

As a Senior Engineer, your output is measured in lines of code, features shipped, bugs fixed, systems designed. As a Lead Engineer, your output is measured in: team velocity, code quality across all engineers, system health, engineering culture, and outcomes for the business. You succeed when your team succeeds, not when you personally write the best code.

This requires a fundamental reorientation: from individual contributor to force multiplier. A Lead who writes great code but neglects mentoring, alignment, and process creates a single point of excellence — not a strong team. A Lead who invests in the team creates compounding returns.

The Three Responsibilities of a Lead

  1. Technical direction: set and maintain the technical vision, make or unblock critical decisions, define standards and patterns
  2. People growth: develop the engineers on your team — through code review, pairing, feedback, stretch assignments, and career conversations
  3. Cross-team alignment: represent the technical perspective to product and business, coordinate with other teams, identify and resolve dependencies

Delegation and Trust

The Lead's most important skill is knowing what to delegate. Delegate too little: you become a bottleneck, your team doesn't grow, you burn out. Delegate too much without investment: quality drops, engineers feel unsupported, trust erodes.

The delegation framework:

  • Delegate tasks that are growth opportunities for the engineer doing them
  • Keep decisions that are irreversible or high-risk — understand them deeply before approving
  • Do not delegate context — ensure engineers have the information to make good decisions
  • Follow up without micromanaging — check in, not check on

Technical Credibility

Lead Engineers must maintain technical credibility — the team trusts their technical judgment because it is demonstrably sound. This means: staying current (reading code, attending design reviews, doing occasional IC work), admitting uncertainty rather than bluffing, and being willing to change positions when presented with better evidence.

Credibility is destroyed by: consistently wrong technical predictions, dismissing technical concerns raised by team members, or claiming expertise you do not have. Once lost, it is very hard to rebuild.

The '1-3-5' Rule for Lead Time

A useful heuristic: spend roughly 1 part doing (IC work, code review, design), 3 parts enabling (unblocking, pairing, alignment, decisions), and 5 parts investing (improving processes, developing people, improving architecture over time). The exact ratio varies by context — but if you are spending 8/9 of your time doing IC work, you are not leading.

storyBeats.text: The most senior enchanter at the Academy was promoted to Lead of the Spell Architecture team. She was brilliant. She kept writing code — the best code anyone had seen. She reviewed every pull request personally. She answered every design question. In six months, the team shipped half what they had before. Nobody else had grown. Every decision waited on her. She had multiplied herself once. She needed to multiply the team.

storyBeats.speaker: Engineering Director Vas
storyBeats.text: The transition to Lead is an identity shift, not a promotion. You do not stop being an engineer — you become an engineer whose primary output is other engineers' work. That requires letting go of being the smartest person in the room, letting go of being the one who writes the elegant solution, and finding satisfaction in watching someone else have that moment.

storyBeats.speaker: Engineering Director Vas
storyBeats.text: Technical credibility is not the same as writing the most code. It comes from good judgment consistently demonstrated over time. Being right about risks. Making good predictions. Knowing what you don't know. A Lead who bluffs their way through a technical question destroys the trust they need to lead. Say 'I don't know, let me find out' — and then find out.

storyBeats.speaker: Engineering Director Vas
storyBeats.text: Delegation without context is abandonment. When you hand off a task, you hand off the full picture: why it matters, what constraints exist, what good looks like, and who to talk to when things are unclear. Engineers who feel set up to fail will stop taking on delegated work. Engineers who feel set up to succeed will grow into taking on more.

learningObjectives: Describe the shift from Senior IC to Lead and explain how the measure of success changes
Apply the three Lead responsibilities (technical direction, people growth, cross-team alignment) to a given scenario
Use the delegation framework to decide what to delegate, what to keep, and how to follow up
Explain how technical credibility is built, maintained, and destroyed
commonMistakes: Continuing to do IC work at Senior level, leaving no time for Lead responsibilities
Delegating tasks without providing the context engineers need to succeed
Asserting confidence on technical questions you are not certain about — erodes credibility when wrong
Measuring your output by your own code quality rather than your team's collective output
assessmentCriteria: Can describe three concrete ways a Lead multiplies team impact rather than individual output
Can identify a delegation anti-pattern (bottleneck, abandonment) and explain the correct approach
Can explain what technical credibility is and name two behaviours that destroy it
Can allocate time across doing/enabling/investing and justify the allocation for a given team context
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the transition from Senior Engineer to Lead Engineer to someone who just got their first Lead title. What actually changes? Why can't you keep doing what made you a great Senior? What does success look like now?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Answer the following leadership scenario questions:

  1. You are a new Lead. An engineer on your team consistently delivers work that passes review but lacks tests. How do you address this? What is the wrong approach and what is the right one?
  2. You have a choice: spend 6 hours implementing a complex feature yourself (high quality, fast) or spend 6 hours pairing with a junior engineer who would take 3 days to do it alone (lower quality initially). What factors determine the right choice and why?
  3. An engineer brings a design to you. It is wrong in two ways you can immediately see. How do you respond, and why does the method matter?
  4. Your team is being asked to own a new service in addition to their existing responsibilities. What questions do you ask before agreeing, and what would cause you to push back?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Addressing missing tests:
   Wrong approach: write the tests yourself (doesn't fix the root cause), or give a harsh code review comment without conversation (damages trust, doesn't build the skill).
   Right approach: have a direct 1:1 conversation — not in PR comments. Ask: 'I've noticed tests aren't included in your PRs. Walk me through your thinking about when you write tests.' This surfaces the cause: do they not know how? Not have time? Not see the value? Address the root cause:
   - If skill gap: pair on writing tests together for one session
   - If time pressure: address the workload or clarify that tests are part of the definition of done
   - If value gap: explain the cost (future bugs, slow changes) with a concrete example from your codebase
   Set a clear expectation and follow up on the next PR.

2. Implement yourself vs pair:
   Factors:
   - Is this engineer in their growth window for this skill? (more valuable to pair)
   - Is the 3-day estimate for this feature or for all future features like it? (pairing pays compound returns)
   - Is there a deadline that makes 3 days genuinely unacceptable? (rare — check if real)
   - How often do tasks like this come up? (if weekly, multiplying the skill is critical)
   Usually: pair. The one-time 6-hour vs 3-day comparison is misleading. An engineer who learns this skill delivers value independently on all future similar tasks. Your 6 hours of pairing might buy 20+ hours of future velocity.
   Exception: genuine emergency, one-off task with no growth value, or the engineer explicitly doesn't want to be taught this right now.

3. Responding to a wrong design:
   Method matters as much as content. A Lead who immediately points out both errors destroys the engineer's confidence in their own judgment and creates dependence.
   Better approach:
   - Ask questions: 'Walk me through how this handles [scenario that exposes the first issue].' Let the engineer discover the problem.
   - If they don't see it, prompt: 'What happens when [edge case]?'
   - On the second issue: 'Before we go to implementation, are there any cases where [relevant concern]?'
   This approach: builds reasoning ability (not just corrects this design), preserves ownership, shows you trust them to find problems when asked the right questions. Direct feedback is fine after they've had a chance to discover issues themselves.

4. Accepting new service ownership:
   Questions to ask:
   - What current work would we de-prioritize to absorb this? (no team has infinite capacity)
   - What is the current state of the service — tech debt, test coverage, documentation?
   - What does 'own' mean — oncall? greenfield features? maintenance only?
   - What is the staffing plan — will we get additional headcount?
   Push back if: the team is already at capacity and nothing is being removed, the service has no documentation or tests (hidden maintenance burden), or 'own' means 24/7 oncall with no additional support for an already-understaffed team.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Write a 'Lead manifesto' — a one-page document you would share with a new team stating: (1) how you make technical decisions, (2) how you run code review, (3) how you think about growth and delegation, (4) what you expect from engineers on the team, and (5) what engineers can expect from you. Be specific — no platitudes.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
A strong Lead manifesto is specific and honest about trade-offs, not a list of values. Example:

(1) Technical decisions: I make reversible decisions quickly and by whoever is closest to the problem. I slow down for irreversible decisions and involve the team — not for consensus, but for better information. I always write down why we chose what we chose (ADR). I am willing to be wrong and will say so publicly.

(2) Code review: I review for correctness, maintainability, and learning — in that order. I ask questions before making assertions. My goal is to make PRs merge faster, not slower. If something is a matter of style preference, I'll note it but won't block on it. If something is a correctness issue, I'll explain why and give a concrete alternative.

(3) Growth and delegation: I will give you work that is slightly beyond your current comfort level. I will give you context, not just tasks. I will check in (not check on). I won't rescue you from productive struggle, but I will tell you when you're stuck so long that asking for help is the right move. I expect you to tell me when a task is unclear.

(4) What I expect: do your best work and ask for help when blocked. Be honest about estimates. Raise concerns early, not the day before a deadline. Write tests. Leave the codebase better than you found it. Tell me when something I'm doing isn't working.

(5) What you can expect from me: technical context for everything I delegate. Honest performance feedback, not just positive reviews. I will fight for your growth opportunities and your time. I will unblock you, not wait for you to unblock yourself. I will admit when I'm wrong.

questions.questionHtml: What is the primary measure of a Lead Engineer's success, as distinct from a Senior Engineer's success?
options: The quality and volume of code they personally write
The number of design reviews they lead
The collective outcomes and growth of their team
The number of production incidents they prevent personally
questions.correctAnswer: The collective outcomes and growth of their team
questions.explanationHtml: A Senior Engineer is measured by their individual technical output. A Lead Engineer is measured by the team's collective outcomes: velocity, quality, system health, team growth. A Lead who writes brilliant code while the team struggles has not led well. A Lead whose team consistently ships high-quality work and grows technically has succeeded — regardless of how much code they personally wrote.

questions.questionHtml: A Lead Engineer reviews every PR personally and approves all design decisions. As the team grows, delivery slows significantly. What is the root problem?
options: The team is not skilled enough to work independently
The Lead has become a bottleneck by not delegating and building team capability
The architecture is too complex for distributed ownership
questions.correctAnswer: The Lead has become a bottleneck by not delegating and building team capability
questions.explanationHtml: This is the classic Lead anti-pattern: scaling bottleneck. When the Lead must personally approve everything, team throughput is bounded by the Lead's time and availability. The fix is not more Lead hours — it is investing time in making engineers capable of independent decision-making: code review standards, documented patterns, pairing, and graduated ownership. The Lead's goal is to make themselves a non-bottleneck.

questions.questionHtml: A Lead confidently answers a technical question in a design review but later realises their answer was wrong. What is the correct next action?
options: Say nothing — one mistake doesn't matter
Correct the record privately with only the affected engineer
Publicly acknowledge the error, state the correct answer, and explain any implications for the design decision
Avoid the topic in future reviews to prevent further embarrassment
questions.correctAnswer: Publicly acknowledge the error, state the correct answer, and explain any implications for the design decision
questions.explanationHtml: Technical credibility is built on demonstrable accuracy and intellectual honesty — not perfection. A Lead who publicly corrects their own mistakes demonstrates the exact behaviour they want from their team (psychological safety, intellectual honesty, accuracy over ego). A Lead who stays silent after a known error has caused the team to proceed on false information, and when the error is discovered later, the credibility damage is worse than an immediate correction.
